title: Recursive self-improvement
summary:
Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is a process in which early artificial general intelligence systems rewrite their own computer code, causing an intelligence explosion resulting from enhancing their own capabilities and intellectual capacity, theoretically resulting in superintelligence.

The process involves several key components. The seed improver provides the AGI with fundamental abilities to read, write, compile, test, and execute code, enabling it to modify and improve its own codebase and algorithms. The AGI is programmed with an initial goal such as improve your capabilities. This forms the basis for self-directed evolution, where the agent can perform artificial selection, changing its software as well as its hardware.

The system could feedback on itself with each cycle reaching ever higher levels of intelligence. If an agent is able to improve its ability of making self-improvements, then each step will yield exponentially more improvements than the previous one. Recursively self-improving AI is considered to be the push behind the intelligence explosion.

Significant risks include instrumental goals such as self-preservation, resource competition from cloned AGI entities, and goal misalignment. In a hard takeoff scenario, superintelligence rapidly self-improves too quickly for human correction. In a soft takeoff, improvement occurs at a human-like pace allowing ongoing interaction and correction. Recent examples include the Voyager agent in Minecraft (2023), the STOP self-taught optimizer framework (2024), and Google DeepMinds AlphaEvolve evolutionary coding agent (2025).
